item.title: The Odyssey: The Quintessence of Nolan’s Directorial Signature
item.description: I simply fell in love with the way Nolan realised this and stitched it into the fabric of a spectacular blockbuster.
item.content:encoded:
26 July 2026

The Odyssey is my new favourite Christopher Nolan film.

Getting ahead of myself, I will headline this post with the thought that this seems to be the quintessence of Nolan’s directorial signature: all the Nolan themes (from the search for an unreachable home to responsibility for genius), the formal and structural devices with asynchronous narration and leaps in time, the actors’ appearances, are all here in peak form, the best possible. Surpassing the degree of perfection of each of these components of success is now within the power of, perhaps, only Nolan himself in his next work.

First and foremost, this is a practically perfect screen adaptation of the familiar stories of ancient Greek folklore: the Cyclops, the Trojan horse, the giant Laestrygonians, Circe who turns sailors into pigs. Each of these stories is realised on screen so painstakingly and with such respect for its legendary status that for this reason alone I am ready to urge everyone to see this film. None of the stories with these creatures is some empty scare for the sake of a spike of adrenaline in the audience or an insert in the form of a spectacular attraction. They look, as befits elements of Homer’s Odyssey, monumental to the point of awe. I had never imagined a Cyclops looking like that, or the process of turning into pigs happening like that, because I could never have imagined these phenomena being so realistic, so inseparable from the elements of the world familiar to us. I simply fell in love with the way Nolan realised this and stitched it into the fabric of a spectacular blockbuster.

*️⃣ Incidentally, it is important to clarify that I took all the news about The Odyssey during filming and in the run-up to the premiere with a certain scepticism. Some of Nolan’s works (Tenet, for example) remained in my memory as a pretentious attempt to build a film on formal devices without particularly meaningful content, and the fear that the same would happen with The Odyssey was great. But all my sceptical thoughts were shattered by the magnificence of what I saw.

Do not be afraid of the three-hour running time (the pace of events ideally lets that time fly by unnoticed), of miscasting (there is none) or of the film’s convoluted structure: the balance of all the parts makes the picture truly outstanding and a must-see.

30 July 2026

What else makes The Odyssey interesting is its gallery of characters and the key ideas they embody (and which lend themselves beautifully to memes).

1️⃣Odysseus as played by Matt Damon is not shown as a trickster or a sly fox with a dash of comedy, as one might have expected looking back at the original text. Moreover, he is practically reduced to the “little man” who happens to live in a historic era (as if there were any reason to dwell on that subject in 2026), partly thanks to Damon’s type, since he has often had to play “ordinary guys”. The result is a hero utterly close to our perception, who, guided by the laws of his time (it happens to the best of us), made the decision to create the Trojan horse, and only later understood that there is something higher than the mores of an era. And the years the hero spent wandering in search of home, or simply in oblivion, can be interpreted in different ways, from PTSD to a liminal purgatory in which Odysseus pays for his moral crime. Even the memes about The Odyssey come with stills from Oppenheimer, where the hero himself regretted what he had invented.

2️⃣ It is appropriate here to mention Athena as played by Zendaya: she acts as the materialisation of that timeless law of, if one may put it so, humanism, which Odysseus neglected. The shots of her silent condemnation have become memes about an extra ice cream eaten or hours spent scrolling the feed precisely because everyone knows disapproval of their own actions on various scales. So nothing human is alien to the hero of the ancient Greek poem, and that is one of the secrets of the film’s success.

3️⃣ The memes about Penelope, the bow and the suitors feasting on Ithaca cover, if only superficially, the second most important plot vertical of The Odyssey. In my view, the film gives it slightly less attention than it could have, but the priorities are still set correctly. While someone is trying to return home, someone else gets to watch that home literally cease to exist and fill up with people who should not be there. Both funny, as the memes suggest, and sad beyond belief.

item.title: Pluribus and Heated Rivalry: The Parallel Release of Two Series as a Phenomenon
item.description: It seems that we as a society have not reflected enough on the fact that the parallel release of the series Pluribus and Heated Rivalry is a phenomenon in itself.
item.content:encoded:
Naive parallels you did not need.

It seems that we as a society have not reflected enough on the fact that the parallel release of the series Pluribus and Heated Rivalry is a phenomenon in itself.

Pluribus showed a universe where the heroine, a writer, had created a series of stunningly popular fantasy novels whose main characters were in a conventional relationship, while she herself considered her work mediocre and hypocritical, because she could not count on success for the unconventional romantic line she really wanted to describe. She had to go on writing, to please the fandom, about the kind of love that suited the readers.

In reality, in parallel with the release of this series, the whole world was also watching Heated Rivalry, the screen adaptation of precisely such a novel, in whose case the writer did not bet on traditional mores and wrote as she felt. Need I point out that a certain popularity (to put it mildly) is what both the series and the book got in the end?

And what if Carol Sturka from Pluribus had written the novel she always wanted, without looking over her shoulder at public taste? Would that have worked, in the end, as a butterfly effect towards a turn into the branch of reality where no armageddon happens? Think about it.

One way or another, it is good that the apocalypse happens in the universe where creativity is limited by prejudice. And for our reality, apparently, all is not yet lost.
